newsitem.title: PANAMA: C&W to invest $572 mln in Panama unit.
newsitem.headline: C&W to invest $572 mln in Panama unit.

text.p: Britain's Cable and Wireless Plc, the new managers of Panama's national telephone company INTEL, pledged Monday to inject $572 million over five years to boost infrastructure and customer service.
The investment "will make revolutionary changes in the telecommunications capability of Panama," C&W Panama chief executive officer,Troy Todd,told reporters.

C&W bid $652 million to secure a 49 percent stake in Panama's National Telecommunications Institute (INTEL) when the group was privatized in May. The joint venture was renamed Cable & Wireless Panama.

"The Board of Directors of Cable & Wireless Panama have agreed an investment plan of $572 million over five years in new infrastructure and customer service, (and) the development of new products and services," C&W said in a separate statement.
Todd said C&W would invest in new switches, line plant and information systems in order to reduce the waiting time for service, as well as improve customer accessibility in urban and rural areas.
C&W has pledged to deliver over 60,000 new lines before March 1998, rising to 400,000 new lines before March 2002, taking the national total to over 700,000.
"At the same time Cable & Wireless will install 10,000 modern payphones throughout the Republic, especially in the interior," C&W said in the statement.

The 20 year concession requires C&W to set up a Band B cellular service within 12 months. Todd said the license and the cost of setting-up the service -- which will directly compete with BellSouth Corp, at the moment Panama's only cellular telephone network -- would exceed $100 million.
The company also said it would put considerable emphasis on training its 3,600 Panama staff.

"The most important point is to develop the employees here so that they can play a wider part in the global operations of C&W and so that C&W Panama can play a part in our global plans," regional executive Bill Allen told Reuters.
Todd said C&W compared Panama's highly developed urban economy to the markets of Hong Kong and Singapore, despite a line penetration of only 12 percent, which offered significant scope for growth.
The contract, which C&W won, calls for making the system 100 percent digital.
C&W is the third largest carrier of international telephone traffic in the world.
(( -- Paul de Bendern, Panama City newsroom, 507-223 7739))
